title: Grandmother of a king (Ruth 4)
hookLine: an immigrant widow becomes great-grandmother of David, in Jesus' family tree

lines: SPREAD THY SKIRT OVER THINE HANDMAID.
HO, SUCH A ONE! SIT DOWN HERE.
cards: A man sits down at the city gate and waits. Here the gate works like a courthouse. In chapter three, Naomi sends Ruth to the threshing floor, and Ruth asks Boaz to spread his skirt over her, "for thou art a near kinsman."
She's asking him to marry her, and to take up the family's cause. Boaz says yes, with one problem: there's a closer relative.
In the morning the closer relative walks past the gate, and Boaz calls out, "Ho, such a one! turn aside, sit down here." Ten elders sit down to watch.

teach.h: GO'EL: THE NEAR KINSMAN WHO REDEEMS.
teach.b: The Hebrew word for this relative is go'el, a redeemer: the near kinsman whose duty is to buy back family land and keep a dead man's name alive. Naomi has a field to sell. Will you redeem it?

I will, says the man. Then Boaz adds: the day you buy the field, you also take Ruth the Moabitess, the dead man's widow. The man backs out: "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance."

teach.h: THE MAN WITH NO NAME BACKS OUT.
teach.b: He passes his shoe to Boaz, the old way of sealing a deal, and the man with no name walks out of the Bible. Boaz marries Ruth, and they have a son. The last words go to the women of the town, speaking to Naomi.
In chapter one she came home empty.

teach.h: BETTER TO THEE THAN SEVEN SONS.
teach.b: Now they say this child will restore her life and nourish her old age, "for thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him."

Better than seven sons, said of a foreign daughter-in-law. Naomi lays the boy in her bosom, and the neighbors name him Obed. Then the book widens in one sentence: "he is the father of Jesse, the father of David."
The Moabite widow who gleaned in a stranger's field is the great-grandmother of Israel's king.
Matthew's family line of Jesus names her too: "Booz begat Obed of Ruth." The genealogy could have listed only fathers. It stops to say her name.
Some readers take that as a sign the outsider was in the story all along.

how: Christians read the end of Ruth together with Matthew 1, where Ruth is named in the family line of Jesus, as part of the story of how God's people came to include those from outside it.

games.why: he says, I cannot redeem it, lest I mar mine own inheritance, and passes his shoe. the text never even gives his name.

practice: Go back through your own line, or your town, to someone who came from somewhere else: a grandparent who crossed a border, a neighbor who learned your language, someone who married into the family and was never quite treated as family.
Let one of them come to mind, and name one thing you have because they came. If you pray, give thanks for them.
